newsitem.title: USA: China envoy highlights Taiwan in ties with U.S..
newsitem.headline: China envoy highlights Taiwan in ties with U.S..

text.p: China's ambassador to the United States has underscored that Taiwan is the most important and sensitive issue in relations between the two countries.

At a conference on Thursday marking the 25th anniversary of the Shanghai communique, which also became an occasion for paying tribute to paramount leader Deng Xiaoping for his role in opening China to the world, Ambassador Li Dao Yu said:
"Let's not forget that the Taiwan question is the most important and sensitive in our relations."

The Shanghai communique was issued at the conclusion of meetings between former U.S. President Richard Nixon and Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai on February 27, 1972, seven years before the two countries established formal diplomatic ties.
"Taiwan is an inseparable part of China," said Li.
"The Taiwan question involves the national feeling of 1.2 billion Chinese people," he continued. "And this brooks no interference from any foreign country."
China has considered Taiwan a renegade province since the two sides split after a civil war in 1949.

Peter Tarnoff, U.S. Acting Secretary of State, also speaking at the conference, reiterated the "enduring commitment" of the United States to the one-China policy, which he said "provides the stability for peaceful settlement of the Taiwan question."
But no single question should put the complex relations between the United States and China on hold to the detriment of both sides, Tarnoff said.

Calling the volatile Korean Peninsula "the most dangerous flashpoint," Tarnoff said it was essential to work with China on regional security. The same cooperation was needed to stop the spread of nuclear proliferation, he added.
With thousands of U.S. citizens residing in Hong Kong and U.S. firms doing business there, the United States will have a signficant stake in Hong Kong's future, Tarnoff said.
Turning to economic relations, Tarnoff said the U.S. trade deficit with China was a "major concern" and China must further open its market before gaining accession to the World Trade Organisation.
Washington's swelling trade deficit with Beijing has long been a sensitive issue between the two sides. China has said its customs figures show a surplus in favour of the U.S.
Henry Kissinger, Secretary of State in 1973-1977, said Deng's retirement from politics three years ago allowed the Chinese leaders to prepare for the transfer of power.
"I believe the transition will be smooth," he said, adding however, "The opaqueness of the political system is carefully preserved."
Kissinger expected the decentralising forces in China would continue with economic modernisation but would pose no threat to China's political unity.
Alexander Haig, Secretary of State in 1981-82, agreed, noting that the Beijing government and the People's Liberation Army were effective in keeping centrifugal forces in check.
